mountain-goat.diet: Alpine grasses, sedges, forbs, woody browse, mosses, and lichens
mountain-goat.shelter: Shallow bedding depressions pawed into cliff ledges and rocky terrain
mountain-goat.preferredHabitat: Steep alpine and subalpine cliffs with escape terrain above turf
mountain-goat.fact: Both sexes grow permanent black horns; you can count the annual rings to age one.
mountain-goat.role: A sure-footed alpine grazer of the highest cliffs, browsing grasses, forbs, and lichens across the rock. Its rubbery-padded hooves grip terrain few predators can follow. Kids and adults are still taken by cougars, and eagles snatch newborns from ledges.

bighorn-sheep.diet: Chiefly grasses and sedges, with forbs and woody browse in winter
bighorn-sheep.shelter: Beds on rocky ledges and rugged escape terrain near cliffs
bighorn-sheep.preferredHabitat: Open grassy mountain slopes beside rugged, rocky cliffs
bighorn-sheep.fact: Bighorns flee across rocky ledges barely a few inches wide to escape predators.
bighorn-sheep.role: A cliff-edge grazer that crops grasses and forbs on open slopes, never far from rugged escape terrain. Rams clash horns in booming rutting contests each fall. Lambs and adults are hunted by cougars, and eagles may take the very young.

pika.diet: Grasses, forbs, and wildflowers, gathered and dried into winter haypiles
pika.shelter: Cool gaps deep within talus and broken rock
pika.preferredHabitat: Talus slopes and rock piles bordering alpine flower meadows
pika.fact: Pikas cut and sun-dry little haystacks of plants to eat beneath the winter snow.
pika.role: A tiny talus-dwelling relative of rabbits and the engine of the alpine food web. It spends summer harvesting haypiles of forbs and grasses to survive under snow. Pikas are hunted by weasels, martens, foxes, and eagles alike.

marmot.diet: Grasses, flowering plants, and seeds in late summer
marmot.shelter: Deep burrow systems dug beneath boulders
marmot.preferredHabitat: Open meadow patches with boulders and burrow ground
marmot.fact: Predation causes about 98% of yellow-bellied marmots' summer deaths.
marmot.role: A stout, sun-loving rodent that grazes meadow plants and fattens on seeds before an eight-month hibernation. Colonies whistle alarm calls from boulder lookouts. They are prime prey for golden eagles, coyotes, and foxes.

snowshoe-hare.diet: Green plants in summer; buds, twigs, bark, and conifer needles in winter
snowshoe-hare.shelter: Shallow forms under dense shrubs and conifer cover
snowshoe-hare.preferredHabitat: Brushy thickets and dense understory near open turf
snowshoe-hare.fact: Its molt from brown to winter white is triggered by day length, not snow.
snowshoe-hare.role: A browsing hare of brushy treeline cover whose coat flips brown-to-white with the seasons. Its numbers cycle roughly every ten years, driving predator populations. Martens, foxes, eagles, and owls all hunt it.

sources.name: USFS Fire Effects Information System - Lepus americanus

elk-alpine.diet: Grasses, sedges, and forbs in summer; browse, bark, and lichens in winter
elk-alpine.shelter: Beds in timber edges and shaded cover beside meadows
elk-alpine.preferredHabitat: High summer meadows near forest cover and snowmelt water
elk-alpine.fact: Elk chase the 'green wave' of new growth up the mountains each summer.
elk-alpine.role: A large migratory grazer that summers in high meadows, following fresh growth uphill and bugling through the autumn rut. Bulls regrow massive antlers yearly. Cougars take adults, while eagles and coyotes may take newborn calves.

mule-deer-alpine.diet: A selective browser of shrubs, forbs, buds, fruits, and lichens
mule-deer-alpine.shelter: Beds in shaded thickets and krummholz cover
mule-deer-alpine.preferredHabitat: High summer meadows and shrublands with clean water
mule-deer-alpine.fact: Mule deer clear obstacles with a bounding, four-footed gait called stotting.
mule-deer-alpine.role: A selective high-country browser that summers in alpine meadows and shrublands before migrating down each fall. It picks the most digestible forbs, buds, and browse. Cougars are its main predator; fawns are also taken by eagles and coyotes.

fox-alpine.diet: Voles, pikas, hares, ground birds and eggs, insects, and berries
fox-alpine.shelter: Earthen dens, often burrows co-opted from other animals
fox-alpine.preferredHabitat: High country with rocky cover and abundant small prey
fox-alpine.fact: Red foxes often move into burrows dug by rabbits or marmots instead of digging.
fox-alpine.role: An adaptable mountain mesopredator that hunts pikas, marmots, and ground birds and rounds out its diet with insects and berries. It listens for prey moving beneath the snow, then dives in headfirst. Golden eagles are its main threat here.

pine-marten.diet: Voles, red squirrels, pikas, hares, birds, eggs, insects, and berries
pine-marten.shelter: Dens in tree cavities, hollow logs, stumps, and rock crevices
pine-marten.preferredHabitat: Structurally complex treeline forest with rocky cover
pine-marten.fact: Pine martens hunt beneath the winter snowpack through tunnels others can't reach.
pine-marten.role: An agile treeline weasel that hunts voles, squirrels, pikas, and young hares, adding berries and insects in season. It ranges over complex forest and rock, even beneath the snowpack. Great horned owls, eagles, and larger carnivores prey on it.

sources.name: Alaska Dept. of Fish & Game - American Marten

ptarmigan.diet: Buds, twigs, leaves, seeds, and flowers; willow is the sole winter food
ptarmigan.shelter: Camouflaged ground scrapes among lichen-covered alpine rocks
ptarmigan.preferredHabitat: Alpine tundra above treeline year-round, wintering in willow basins
ptarmigan.fact: It is the only North American bird living entirely above treeline all year.
ptarmigan.role: A superbly camouflaged alpine grouse that grazes buds, leaves, and seeds, surviving winter almost entirely on willow. It grows feathered 'snowshoes' on its feet each winter. Eagles, foxes, weasels, and martens all hunt it and its chicks.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds - White-tailed Ptarmigan

clarks-nutcracker.diet: Pine seeds cached by the thousand, plus insects and small animals
clarks-nutcracker.shelter: Cup nest in conifer branches, sited near winter seed caches
clarks-nutcracker.preferredHabitat: High conifer forest and treeline near pine-seed sources
clarks-nutcracker.fact: It can relocate thousands of buried seed caches months later, even under snow.
clarks-nutcracker.role: A mountain corvid that harvests and buries thousands of pine seeds, replanting the very forests it depends on. Its cached hoard lets it breed in deep winter. It also takes insects and small vertebrates when available.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds - Clark's Nutcracker

golden-eagle.diet: Marmots, hares, ground squirrels, ptarmigan and other birds, plus carrion
golden-eagle.shelter: Huge stick eyries on cliffs and steep escarpments
golden-eagle.preferredHabitat: Open, high country with cliffs and abundant medium prey
golden-eagle.fact: Golden eagles sometimes line their nests with aromatic leaves, perhaps to deter insects.
golden-eagle.role: The apex hunter of the high country, taking marmots, hares, and ptarmigan and even smaller carnivores in powerful stoops. It arrives only when the mountain teems with prey. Adults have essentially no predators.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds - Golden Eagle
Birds of the World - Golden Eagle Food Habits

alpine-butterfly.diet: Larvae eat stonecrop; adults sip nectar from Sedum and daisy-family flowers
alpine-butterfly.shelter: No nest; larvae shelter in leaf litter and rocks, overwintering as eggs
alpine-butterfly.preferredHabitat: Rocky open alpine and montane slopes where stonecrop grows
alpine-butterfly.fact: Its pale red-and-black wings warn predators that it tastes unpalatable.
alpine-butterfly.role: A hardy alpine butterfly whose caterpillars feed only on stonecrop while adults nectar across the meadow flowers. Its aposematic wings advertise a foul taste. Birds and spiders that ignore the warning still catch some.

sources.name: Butterflies and Moths of North America - Parnassius smintheus

bumblebee-alpine.diet: Nectar and pollen from deep-throated alpine flowers
bumblebee-alpine.shelter: Colonial nests in ground cavities and old rodent burrows
bumblebee-alpine.preferredHabitat: High alpine and boreal flower meadows, often above treeline
bumblebee-alpine.fact: This bee's tongue grew measurably shorter from 1966 to 2014 as flowers declined.
bumblebee-alpine.role: A cold-tolerant, long-tongued bumblebee that pollinates deep alpine blossoms, shivering its flight muscles to fly in near-freezing air. Its colonies nest underground. Birds, crab spiders, and robber flies prey on foragers.

sources.name: Molecular Ecology - Alpine bumblebee tongue-length study

snowmelt-trout.diet: Aquatic and terrestrial insects; larger fish add small fish to the diet
snowmelt-trout.shelter: Cold, clear pools and undercut banks; gravel riffles for spawning
snowmelt-trout.preferredHabitat: Cold, clear, connected snowmelt streams and mountain lakes
snowmelt-trout.fact: A poor competitor, native cutthroat are displaced by introduced brown and brook trout.
snowmelt-trout.role: A cold-water native whose presence signals a clean, healthy mountain stream. It picks off drifting insects and, when large, smaller fish. It is threatened by non-native trout that out-compete and prey on it.

rosy-finch.diet: Tiny alpine plant seeds and insects, often gleaned off snowfields
rosy-finch.shelter: Bulky cup of moss and grass tucked into a cliff crack or talus
rosy-finch.preferredHabitat: Alpine zones above treeline: talus, scree, cliffs, and glaciers
rosy-finch.fact: It nests higher than nearly any other songbird in North America.
rosy-finch.role: A high-altitude songbird that hops across snow and talus gathering wind-borne seeds and chilled insects. It nests in rock crevices above treeline. Falcons and hawks are its main predators.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds - Gray-crowned Rosy-Finch

american-pipit.diet: Mostly insects and their larvae, plus spiders and some seeds
american-pipit.shelter: Ground nest of grass tucked beside a rock or vegetation clump
american-pipit.preferredHabitat: Open alpine meadows and tundra in the breeding season
american-pipit.fact: It forages at snowbank edges for insects chilled after drifting up from below.
american-pipit.role: A slender ground-walking songbird of open alpine meadows that constantly bobs its tail as it hunts insects. It gleans chilled prey from snowbank margins. Hawks and nest raiders are its chief threats.

sources.name: Birds of the World - American Pipit Food Habits

ermine.diet: Small rodents, especially voles; also pikas, birds, eggs, and insects
ermine.shelter: Dens in prey burrows, rock piles, and hollow logs, lined with fur
ermine.preferredHabitat: Talus and shrubby edges near meadows with dense rodent prey
ermine.fact: Its coat turns pure white in winter except for a jet-black tail tip.
ermine.role: A small, fierce weasel that specializes in voles and other rodents, also taking young pikas and ground-bird eggs. It hunts prey burrows it can slip right into. Foxes, martens, and raptors prey on it in turn.

sources.name: Idaho Fish and Game - Mustela erminea

boreal-toad.diet: Beetles, ants, flies, and other invertebrates; tadpoles graze algae
boreal-toad.shelter: Burrows, rodent holes, logs, and rocks in moist cover near pools
boreal-toad.preferredHabitat: Subalpine and alpine wet meadows with open breeding pools
boreal-toad.fact: Rocky Mountain boreal toads have crashed from the deadly amphibian chytrid fungus.
boreal-toad.role: The high country's only toad, an insect-eating amphibian that breeds in shallow snowmelt pools and takes years to mature. Its tadpoles graze algae. Chytrid fungus has devastated southern populations, making it a conservation flagship.

mountain-bluebird.diet: Mostly insects caught in flight; berries and seeds in colder months
mountain-bluebird.shelter: Old woodpecker holes, natural cavities, and nest boxes
mountain-bluebird.preferredHabitat: Open high meadows with scattered trees and hunting perches
mountain-bluebird.fact: It cannot dig its own hole, so it reuses old woodpecker cavities and nest boxes.
mountain-bluebird.role: A brilliant sky-blue thrush of open high meadows that hover-hunts insects on the wing and adds berries in the cold. As a cavity nester it depends on old woodpecker holes. Hawks and cavity raiders prey on it.

alpine-chipmunk.diet: Seeds of sedges, forbs, and grasses, plus berries, fungi, pine seeds, and eggs
alpine-chipmunk.shelter: Nests deep in crevices between talus rocks and boulders
alpine-chipmunk.preferredHabitat: High talus slopes and rocky meadows of the Sierra Nevada
alpine-chipmunk.fact: It ranges higher than almost any other chipmunk, up to 3,900 meters.
alpine-chipmunk.role: A tiny, high-altitude seed-eater that caches seeds and helps disperse alpine plants across the talus. It also raids the eggs of rosy-finches and sparrows. Foxes, weasels, martens, and raptors all hunt it, tying it into the predator web.

cascades-frog.diet: An aquatic and semiaquatic insectivore, taking insects and spiders
cascades-frog.shelter: Snowmelt ponds and lakes; hibernates in soil under lake bottoms
cascades-frog.preferredHabitat: Cold high-country ponds and streams near coniferous forest
cascades-frog.fact: It stays active in near-freezing snowmelt water and basks on wet rocks.
cascades-frog.role: A cold-adapted mountain frog that eats insects and spiders while its tadpoles graze algae in snowmelt pools. It links pond invertebrates to larger predators. Introduced trout eat its tadpoles, driving steep declines across its southern range.

mountain-chickadee.diet: Insects and spiders in summer; conifer seeds and nuts in fall and winter
mountain-chickadee.shelter: Old woodpecker holes and natural cavities in conifers and aspen
mountain-chickadee.preferredHabitat: High evergreen forests of pine, fir, and spruce in the West
mountain-chickadee.fact: It caches thousands of seeds and remembers where it hid them.
mountain-chickadee.role: A busy conifer-forest insectivore that gleans insects from twigs and switches to cached pine seeds in winter. Often the nucleus of mixed foraging flocks, it disperses conifer seeds. Small hawks, weasels, and martens prey on it and its nestlings.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds - Mountain Chickadee

pine-grosbeak.diet: Buds, seeds, and fruits of conifers and shrubs; some insects in summer
pine-grosbeak.shelter: Concealed cup nest near the trunk of a dense conifer
pine-grosbeak.preferredHabitat: Open subalpine spruce, fir, and pine forest near timberline
pine-grosbeak.fact: A plump, unhurried finch of the cold high forests, nipping buds and needles.
pine-grosbeak.role: A large, sluggish finch that lives almost entirely on conifer buds, seeds, and fruits, adding insects to feed its young. It helps disperse tree and shrub seeds. Martens, small raptors, and foxes prey on it, especially at nests.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds - Pine Grosbeak

white-crowned-sparrow.diet: Mainly weed and grass seeds, plus caterpillars, beetles, and other insects
white-crowned-sparrow.shelter: Ground or low-shrub cup nest among mosses, lichens, and heath
white-crowned-sparrow.preferredHabitat: Krummholz edges, alpine meadows, and heath with bare ground
white-crowned-sparrow.fact: Young white-crowns learn their song dialect from the neighbours nearby.
white-crowned-sparrow.role: A ground-foraging sparrow of alpine meadow and krummholz edges that eats seeds and summer insects. It disperses seeds and feeds insect larvae to its chicks. Foxes, weasels, and martens hunt the adults and raid its low nests.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds - White-crowned Sparrow

tree-squirrel.diet: Acorns, nuts, seeds, tree buds, and fungi; occasional insects and bird eggs
tree-squirrel.shelter: Tree cavity dens and leaf-and-twig dreys built high in the canopy
tree-squirrel.preferredHabitat: Mature deciduous or mixed forest rich in oaks and hickories
tree-squirrel.fact: Gray squirrels scatter-hoard thousands of nuts each year, and the caches they forget grow into new trees.
tree-squirrel.role: Tree squirrels are major seed predators and accidental seed dispersers whose buried, forgotten nuts regenerate the forest canopy. They also spread mycorrhizal fungal spores and occasionally raid bird nests. As abundant prey they feed nearly every forest mesopredator and raptor.

woodpecker.diet: Mostly insects—beetle larvae, ants, caterpillars—with some berries, seeds, and sap
woodpecker.shelter: Self-excavated cavities in standing deadwood; roosts in cavities year-round
woodpecker.preferredHabitat: Open deciduous and mixed woodland with dead snags full of insects
woodpecker.fact: Downy woodpeckers are small enough to hammer into goldenrod galls for fly larvae that larger woodpeckers can't reach.
woodpecker.role: Woodpeckers regulate wood-boring beetles and bark insects, easing pest pressure on trees. Their abandoned cavities house nuthatches, wrens, and flying squirrels, making them ecosystem engineers. They feed hawks, owls, and nest-raiding squirrels and snakes.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Downy Woodpecker

forest-salamander.diet: Small invertebrates: mites, springtails, spiders, beetles, ants, and earthworms
forest-salamander.shelter: Under logs, rocks, and moist leaf litter; retreats into soil burrows
forest-salamander.preferredHabitat: Cool, damp deciduous forest floor with abundant woody debris
forest-salamander.fact: In some eastern forests the combined weight of these tiny lungless salamanders exceeds that of all the birds.
forest-salamander.role: Red-backed salamanders are a keystone of the forest-floor detritus web, controlling the mites and springtails that break down leaf litter. Their huge collective biomass makes them a key food subsidy for snakes, birds, and small mammals. They breathe through their skin, so they signal forest moisture and soil health.

great-horned-owl.diet: Mammals and birds—rabbits, voles, squirrels, chipmunks, skunks—plus reptiles and frogs
great-horned-owl.shelter: Adopts old hawk, crow, or heron stick nests in large trees; also snags and ledges
great-horned-owl.preferredHabitat: Mature forest broken by open ground, across nearly every biome
great-horned-owl.fact: Great horned owls are among the only predators that routinely kill and eat skunks, seemingly unbothered by the spray.
great-horned-owl.role: The great horned owl sits at the top of the nocturnal forest food web, with the most varied prey base of any North American raptor. It regulates rabbits, squirrels, chipmunks, and even other owls, so its loss lets prey populations surge. Adults have essentially no predators; only eggs and young are vulnerable.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Great Horned Owl

black-bear.diet: Berries, nuts, grasses, and forbs; insects, fish, and carrion; fawns opportunistically
black-bear.shelter: Dens in hollow trees, root masses, rock crevices, or dug cavities; hibernates in winter
black-bear.preferredHabitat: Dense forest with thick understory and abundant berry and nut mast
black-bear.fact: Black bear cubs are born during hibernation weighing under half a pound—the smallest newborns relative to adult size of any placental mammal.
black-bear.role: Black bears are generalist omnivores that disperse berry seeds, dig up and regulate colonial insects, and opportunistically take deer fawns and elk calves. As the most abundant large carnivore in North American forests, they link the mast, insect, and vertebrate food layers at once. Adults have essentially no natural predators.

red-fox-forest.diet: Rodents, rabbits, birds, and reptiles; insects, fruit, and carrion
red-fox-forest.shelter: Earthen dens dug into slopes or taken over from other animals, reused for generations
red-fox-forest.preferredHabitat: Forest edges and scrub-woodland mixes; avoids dense unbroken forest
red-fox-forest.fact: Red foxes have around 28 distinct calls, and each individual's voice is recognizable to other foxes.
red-fox-forest.role: The red fox is a versatile mesopredator that keeps small rodents, rabbits, and ground-nesting birds in check while dispersing seeds through the fruit it eats. It sits below apex predators like bears and bobcats and above the small mammals it hunts. Fox pairs often reuse and expand the same den site across generations.

sources.name: National Wildlife Federation — Raccoon (fox as predator)

mule-deer-forest.diet: Browser: leaves, twigs, and forbs in summer; woody browse, acorns, and berries in winter
mule-deer-forest.shelter: No fixed den; beds in dense shrubs and forest cover for warmth and safety
mule-deer-forest.preferredHabitat: Forest edges and open woodland with shrubby browse and water
mule-deer-forest.fact: A bounding mule deer releases an alarm scent from its hind legs that alerts every nearby deer at once.
mule-deer-forest.role: Mule deer are key large browsers that shape the forest understory and the regeneration of shrubs and young conifers. They form a critical prey base for large carnivores, while their fawns feed bobcats, foxes, and bears. Seasonal migrations move nutrients across the landscape.

elk-forest.diet: Grasses, sedges, and forbs in summer; woody browse and bark in winter
elk-forest.shelter: No fixed shelter; calves hidden in dense vegetation; the herd shares vigilance
elk-forest.preferredHabitat: Grassy clearings and open woodland edges within larger forest
elk-forest.fact: In Yellowstone, elk make up about 85% of winter wolf kills and their carcasses feed at least a dozen scavenger species.
elk-forest.role: Elk are a dominant large herbivore whose heavy grazing shapes grasslands, willows, and aspen; their decline lets vegetation rebound. As the primary prey of wolves, cougars, and bears, they anchor the large-predator food web, and their carcasses sustain a broad scavenger guild. Migrations redistribute nutrients across elevations.

raccoon.diet: Opportunistic: crayfish, insects, frogs, fish, small mammals, bird eggs, fruit, and nuts
raccoon.shelter: Hollow tree dens preferred; also rock crevices, burrows, and structures
raccoon.preferredHabitat: Moist forest near water for foraging and dabbling
raccoon.fact: A raccoon's sensitive forepaws carry about four times more touch receptors than its eyes have light receptors.
raccoon.role: Raccoons are adaptable omnivores that regulate crayfish, frogs, and invertebrates while dispersing fruit seeds and preying on bird nests. Their high density makes them a major mid-trophic connector between the aquatic and forest webs. Coyotes, large owls, and bobcats keep them in the mesopredator tier.

porcupine.diet: Strict herbivore: inner bark in winter; buds, twigs, leaves, and mast in warmer months
porcupine.shelter: Rock dens, hollow logs, and tree canopies; reuses the same dens seasonally
porcupine.preferredHabitat: Coniferous and mixed forest with trees offering edible bark
porcupine.fact: The fisher is one of the only predators able to kill porcupines, flipping them to reach the quill-free belly.
porcupine.role: Porcupines are ecosystem engineers whose bark-stripping kills or deforms trees, creating snags for cavity nesters and diversifying forest structure. Their mast feeding competes with deer and squirrels. They are the main prey base for fishers and a supplemental meal for bobcats and bears.

bobcat.diet: Obligate carnivore: rabbits, rodents, squirrels, and deer fawns; some birds and reptiles
bobcat.shelter: Dens in hollow logs, brush piles, thickets, and rock crevices
bobcat.preferredHabitat: Forest with dense understory, brushland, and rocky terrain
bobcat.fact: In the eastern U.S. bobcat numbers rise and fall closely with the local cottontail rabbit supply.
bobcat.role: Bobcats are keystone mesopredators that suppress rabbits, rodents, and squirrels, easing browsing pressure on forest plants. As mid-level hunters they sit below cougars and wolves and above the small mammals they take. They help structure entire small-mammal communities.

chipmunk.diet: Seeds, nuts, and fruit, plus insects, worms, slugs, fungi, and occasional bird eggs
chipmunk.shelter: Underground burrows up to 10 m long with nest and food-storage chambers
chipmunk.preferredHabitat: Mature deciduous forest with logs, stumps, and rocky cover
chipmunk.fact: Chipmunks don't truly hibernate—they wake through winter to eat from seed caches holding over a liter of food.
chipmunk.role: Chipmunks are important scatter-hoarders that disperse tree seeds and fungal spores, aiding forest regeneration. They eat many insects in summer and, as abundant prey, feed a wide guild of predators from weasels to owls. Their burrows aerate soil and shelter other small animals.

nuthatch.diet: Insects and spiders in summer; seeds, acorns, and cached nuts through winter
nuthatch.shelter: Tree cavities and old woodpecker holes in mature hardwoods; also nest boxes
nuthatch.preferredHabitat: Mature deciduous and mixed forest with large oaks and hickories
nuthatch.fact: Nuthatches sweep smelly insects around their nest hole, apparently to mask their scent from squirrels.
nuthatch.role: Nuthatches prey on bark-dwelling insects, including tent caterpillars and wood borers, helping check forest pests. By wedging and caching acorns and seeds in bark they aid short-distance seed dispersal. They bridge the insect and seed layers and serve as prey for hawks and owls.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — White-breasted Nuthatch

garter-snake-forest.diet: Earthworms, amphibians, and slugs; also leeches, fish, insects, and small rodents
garter-snake-forest.shelter: Communal winter dens in burrows and rock piles; hides under logs and rocks
garter-snake-forest.preferredHabitat: Moist forest edges and riparian zones near ponds and streams
garter-snake-forest.fact: Garter snakes are the main predator of the toxic rough-skinned newt, and some have evolved resistance to its poison.
garter-snake-forest.role: Garter snakes are generalist mid-web predators that suppress earthworms, slugs, amphibians, and small fish. In the Pacific Northwest they are the key check on rough-skinned newts, and their toxin resistance makes them a famous coevolutionary node. They are important prey for raptors, corvids, and larger predators.

banana-slug.diet: Dead leaves, fungi, decaying matter, and animal scat; occasional live seedlings
banana-slug.shelter: Under logs and bark; seals into a mucus cocoon during dry spells
banana-slug.preferredHabitat: Cool, shaded, persistently moist Pacific forest floor
banana-slug.fact: Banana slugs pass viable seeds and fungal spores through their gut, seeding plants and mycorrhizal networks as they crawl.
banana-slug.role: Banana slugs are primary decomposers that break down leaf litter and scat, returning nutrients to the soil. They disperse seeds and mycorrhizal spores, partnering with both plants and the fungal networks that feed forest trees. Their numbing mucus deters most predators, leaving garter snakes and shrews as the main consumers.

pileated-woodpecker.diet: Carpenter ants and wood-boring beetle larvae; also termites, berries, and nuts
pileated-woodpecker.shelter: Excavates a new rectangular nest cavity each year in large dead snags
pileated-woodpecker.preferredHabitat: Mature and old-growth forest with big standing snags and downed logs
pileated-woodpecker.fact: Its deep rectangular excavations can be large enough to snap a small tree in half.
pileated-woodpecker.role: The pileated woodpecker is a keystone ecosystem engineer whose big cavities become homes for wood ducks, flying squirrels, fishers, bats, and barred owls. It regulates carpenter ant and beetle populations and opens decaying wood to fungi and decomposers. It sits as a secondary consumer and feeds raptors and mustelids.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Pileated Woodpecker

pacific-wren.diet: Beetles, caterpillars, ants, flies, spiders, and millipedes; some winter berries
pacific-wren.shelter: Domed nests low in upturned roots, decaying logs, and stream banks
pacific-wren.preferredHabitat: Old-growth conifer forest with dense understory near streams
pacific-wren.fact: Pacific wren numbers along streams rise with salmon runs, whose nutrients boost the insects the wrens eat.
pacific-wren.role: The Pacific wren is a secondary consumer that suppresses understory invertebrates in old-growth forest, passing that energy up to hawks, corvids, and weasels. Its dependence on damp, log-strewn old growth and salmon-fed streams makes it a living indicator of both forest and watershed health. It nests low in root tangles and rotting wood.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Pacific Wren

rough-skinned-newt.diet: Insects, earthworms, slugs, snails, and amphibian and fish eggs
rough-skinned-newt.shelter: Under rotting logs, rocks, and leaf litter; in ponds during breeding season
rough-skinned-newt.preferredHabitat: Pacific conifer forest near still or slow water
rough-skinned-newt.fact: Its skin holds enough tetrodotoxin to kill several adults, driving a famous poison arms race with garter snakes.
rough-skinned-newt.role: The rough-skinned newt is a mid-trophic consumer of insects, worms, and amphibian eggs, shaping wetland invertebrate and amphibian communities. Its potent tetrodotoxin defense drives adaptive evolution in resistant garter snakes, one of biology's best-known coevolutionary arms races. The toxin leaves it nearly free from most other predators.

sources.name: USGS — Barred Owl predation on Taricha granulosa

northern-flying-squirrel.diet: Mostly underground truffle fungi; also lichens, seeds, nuts, fruit, and insects
northern-flying-squirrel.shelter: Tree cavities, old woodpecker holes, and branch dreys; huddles in winter groups
northern-flying-squirrel.preferredHabitat: Closed-canopy mature conifer forest rich in mycorrhizal fungi
northern-flying-squirrel.fact: Fungal spores turn up in nearly every flying squirrel dropping, making it the forest's key truffle disperser.
northern-flying-squirrel.role: The northern flying squirrel is a keystone mutualist, the main disperser of underground mycorrhizal fungi that conifers depend on for nutrients. This squirrel-fungi-tree partnership underpins forest regeneration. It is also a prime prey item for owls, martens, and fishers, funneling energy from the fungal layer up to top predators.

sources.name: USDA Forest Service — Meyer et al. 2005 (truffle spore dispersal)

wood-duck.diet: Acorns, seeds, and aquatic plants; ducklings and spring birds also eat insects and snails
wood-duck.shelter: Obligate cavity nester in tree holes and nest boxes near water
wood-duck.preferredHabitat: Bottomland hardwood and wooded swamps with slow water and cavity trees
wood-duck.fact: A day after hatching, wood duck ducklings leap from nest cavities up to 50 feet high and land unhurt.
wood-duck.role: Wood ducks are omnivorous consumers linking bottomland forest and wetland food webs, dispersing acorn and aquatic-plant seeds and regulating shallow-water invertebrates. As prey they feed great horned owls, mink, raccoons, and snapping turtles. Depending on woodpecker cavities, their abundance signals healthy wooded wetlands.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Wood Duck

barred-owl.diet: Small mammals, birds, amphibians, reptiles, fish, and invertebrates
barred-owl.shelter: Large tree cavities in mature forest; also old hawk, crow, or squirrel nests
barred-owl.preferredHabitat: Mature mixed or conifer forest near water with large cavity trees
barred-owl.fact: Barred owls sometimes wade into shallow water to catch fish—unusual hunting for a woodland owl.
barred-owl.role: The barred owl is a mid-level predator that regulates mice, voles, chipmunks, squirrels, and amphibians. It sits between small prey and the apex great horned owl, which is its main predator. Its need for large cavity trees makes it an indicator of mature forest health.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Barred Owl

fisher.diet: Small and medium mammals—porcupines, hares, squirrels, mice; also birds and fruit
fisher.shelter: Dens in hollow trees, logs, stumps, and ground burrows; young in high tree cavities
fisher.preferredHabitat: Dense conifer and mixed forest with high canopy closure and hollow trees
fisher.fact: The fisher is one of the only predators that regularly kills porcupines, slashing the face until it can flip it over.
fisher.role: The fisher is a powerful mid-level forest predator and one of the few checks on porcupine numbers, which otherwise damage timber. It partly fills the niche of vanished apex predators, and its presence signals mature, connected forest. Young fishers are prey for bobcats, foxes, and lynx.

little-brown-bat.diet: Strict insectivore: midges, caddisflies, mayflies, moths, beetles, and mosquitoes
little-brown-bat.shelter: Roosts in tree hollows, under bark, and in buildings; hibernates in caves and mines
little-brown-bat.preferredHabitat: Forested land near streams, ponds, and openings for aerial feeding
little-brown-bat.fact: White-nose syndrome, a cold-loving fungus, has wiped out over 90% of little brown bats at many hibernation sites.
little-brown-bat.role: Little brown bats are voracious insectivores, each eating up to half its body weight in insects a night and suppressing forest and aquatic pests. They are a mid-web link between the insect layer and larger predators like owls, fishers, and snakes. White-nose syndrome has caused catastrophic declines.

ensatina.diet: Invertebrates: worms, ants, beetles, spiders, centipedes, millipedes, and snails
ensatina.shelter: Under rocks, bark, and logs on the forest floor; retreats underground when dry
ensatina.preferredHabitat: Moist, shaded forest floor rich in coarse woody debris
ensatina.fact: Ensatinas are lungless, breathing through their skin, and can drop a wriggling, poison-laced tail to escape.
ensatina.role: The ensatina is an abundant forest-floor predator that suppresses decomposer invertebrates like centipedes, millipedes, and sowbugs, linking the detritus web to vertebrate predators. Being lungless, it depends on damp, intact forest, making it an indicator of forest-floor moisture. It is prey for garter snakes, raccoons, and jays.

spotted-towhee.diet: Insects and invertebrates in summer; seeds, acorns, and berries in fall and winter
spotted-towhee.shelter: Dense shrubby thickets and brushy edges; nests on or near the ground
spotted-towhee.preferredHabitat: Brushy forest edges and chaparral with deep leaf litter
spotted-towhee.fact: The spotted towhee feeds with a two-footed backward hop that flicks leaf litter aside to expose food.
spotted-towhee.role: The spotted towhee is an omnivorous ground forager that bridges the invertebrate and seed layers, eating ground beetles and caterpillars in summer and dispersing seeds in winter. Its ground nesting leaves it vulnerable to foxes, raccoons, and snakes, while hawks and owls take adults. It helps turn over and recycle forest-floor litter.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Spotted Towhee

tidepool-crab.diet: Mostly algae, plus detritus, worms, snails, and carrion
tidepool-crab.preferredHabitat: Rocky tidepools and intertidal splash zone
tidepool-crab.fact: Striped shore crabs graze algae but will scavenge and even turn cannibal after molting.
tidepool-crab.role: An abundant intertidal grazer-scavenger that keeps rock surfaces clear of algae and recycles carrion. It is a key prey item for gulls, shorebirds, and larger crabs, linking algae to higher predators.

hermit-crab.preferredHabitat: Tidepools with a supply of empty shells
hermit-crab.fact: When a better shell appears, hermit crabs line up by size and swap shells down the chain.
hermit-crab.role: A tidepool scavenger that cleans up algae and carrion and recycles empty snail shells as portable armor. It is common prey for gulls, fish, and octopus in the intertidal food web.

sea-star.diet: Mussels, barnacles, limpets, chitons, and snails
sea-star.fact: The classic keystone predator: removing it lets mussels overrun the whole shore.
sea-star.role: The textbook keystone predator of the rocky shore. By eating mussels it sets the mussel bed's lower limit and keeps space open for many other species, maintaining intertidal biodiversity.

anemone.diet: Crabs, detached mussels, and small fish stung by its tentacles
anemone.shelter: Tidepool walls, often below mussel beds
anemone.preferredHabitat: Clear, surge-fed tidepools near mussel beds
anemone.fact: Its green glow comes from algae living inside its tissues that share sugars.
anemone.role: A sit-and-wait carnivore of tidepools that ambushes prey washed off the rocks, while also farming symbiotic algae for extra food. It is a minor predator that helps recycle dislodged shellfish and crabs.

sources.name: Monterey Bay Aquarium - Giant green anemone

mussel.shelter: Dense beds anchored to wave-washed rock
mussel.preferredHabitat: Exposed rocky shore with clean moving water
mussel.fact: A single mussel filters several liters of seawater an hour as it feeds.
mussel.role: A reef-building filter feeder whose beds create habitat for countless small animals. It is the key prey that ties together the shore's top predators, from ochre sea stars to sea otters and oystercatchers.

clam.preferredHabitat: Stable sand and gravel near tidepools
clam.fact: You can estimate a littleneck clam's age by counting the growth rings on its shell.
clam.role: A buried filter feeder that helps clean coastal water and stores energy in sheltered sediment. It is important prey for sea otters, shorebirds, crabs, and gulls that dig or crack it open.

sources.name: Animal Diversity Web - Enhydra lutris (predation on clams)

shorebird.diet: Sand crustaceans, mole crabs, and kelp-fly larvae
shorebird.shelter: Shallow scrapes hidden on open sand
shorebird.preferredHabitat: Undisturbed sandy beaches and dune edges
shorebird.fact: Snowy plover chicks can run and feed themselves within hours of hatching.
shorebird.role: A small beach forager that snaps up tiny crustaceans and kelp flies along the tide line. A threatened species and sensitive indicator of quiet, undisturbed beach; its nests fail easily where beaches are busy.

sources.name: All About Birds - Snowy Plover Life History

gull.diet: Fish, crabs, clams, sea stars, and carrion
gull.shelter: Open beach, rocky points, and islands
gull.preferredHabitat: Any shoreline with food to scavenge or catch
gull.fact: Western gulls crack clams by dropping them from the air onto rocks below.
gull.role: A bold generalist that scavenges carrion and preys on crabs, shellfish, and even sea stars, cleaning the beach and linking many prey to the top of the food web. Foxes and coyotes take gulls and their eggs on land.

sources.name: All About Birds - Western Gull Life History

pelican.shelter: Quiet roosts on rocks and sandbars
pelican.preferredHabitat: Fish-rich nearshore water with quiet roosts
pelican.fact: Brown pelicans plunge-dive from up to 65 feet, twisting to protect the neck on impact.
pelican.role: A plunge-diving fish specialist whose recovery after DDT is a major conservation success. Its presence signals healthy schools of forage fish like anchovies in nearshore water.

sources.name: All About Birds - Brown Pelican Life History

cormorant.diet: Small fish, plus crabs and shrimp chased underwater
cormorant.preferredHabitat: Rocky shore with clear diving water
cormorant.fact: Cormorant feathers soak through on purpose, so less buoyancy makes them better divers.
cormorant.role: A pursuit-diving fish hunter that works rocky reefs and the water column. It depends on clear water and healthy fish stocks, so thriving cormorants signal a productive rocky shore.

sources.name: All About Birds - Pelagic Cormorant Life History

sea-turtle.diet: Mostly seagrass and algae as adults; omnivorous when young
sea-turtle.shelter: Offshore waters; nests on quiet sand
sea-turtle.preferredHabitat: Clean shallow water with seagrass and undisturbed beach
sea-turtle.fact: Green sea turtles return to nest on the very beach where they hatched decades earlier.
sea-turtle.role: The only mostly herbivorous sea turtle; adults graze seagrass and algae, keeping beds healthy, while juveniles start as omnivores. Its nesting success is a strong indicator of clean water and undisturbed beaches.

harbor-seal.diet: Fish, plus squid, octopus, and crustaceans
harbor-seal.preferredHabitat: Calm, clean water with undisturbed haul-out shore
harbor-seal.fact: Harbor seals can sleep underwater, surfacing to breathe without fully waking.
harbor-seal.role: A generalist marine predator that eats whatever fish is abundant and easy to catch. Sharks and killer whales are its main predators offshore, but on this restored coast it sits near the top of the food web.

sea-otter.diet: Sea urchins, crabs, mussels, clams, and other shellfish
sea-otter.preferredHabitat: Kelp forest and rocky shore with abundant shellfish
sea-otter.fact: Sea otters wrap up in kelp before sleeping so they don't drift away.
sea-otter.role: A keystone species: by eating sea urchins it stops them overgrazing kelp, letting kelp forests and the life they shelter thrive. It also preys heavily on mussels and clams along the rocky shore.

dolphin.fact: Bottlenose dolphins call each other by name, using signature whistles unique to each one.
dolphin.role: A clever, cooperative predator that herds fish and hunts squid in nearshore water. Larger sharks and orcas can prey on it, but in this roster it is a top predator whose presence marks a lively, fish-rich coast.

migrating-whale.diet: Amphipods and other tiny bottom crustaceans, sifted from sediment
migrating-whale.shelter: Open ocean; passes close to healthy shores
migrating-whale.preferredHabitat: Seen offshore from a fully restored coast
migrating-whale.fact: Gray whales migrate up to 14,000 miles round trip, among the longest of any mammal.
migrating-whale.role: A bottom-feeding baleen whale that rolls on its side to suck up sediment and filter out tiny crustaceans. Killer whales are its main predator; a passing gray whale is a sign of a fully restored, productive coast.

sanderling.diet: Small crabs, amphipods, worms, and mollusks
sanderling.shelter: Open beach above the surf line
sanderling.preferredHabitat: Sandy surf line and wave-washed beach
sanderling.fact: Sanderlings chase retreating waves in busy little sprints to grab stranded invertebrates.
sanderling.role: A wave-chasing sandpiper that feeds on small crustaceans and worms churned up by the surf. Falcons are a key predator, and its winter flocks track the health of open sandy beaches.

sources.name: All About Birds - Sanderling Life History

black-oystercatcher.diet: Mussels and limpets, plus whelks and crabs
black-oystercatcher.shelter: Rocky shore ledges just above the tide
black-oystercatcher.preferredHabitat: Rocky intertidal reefs and tidepool shores
black-oystercatcher.fact: Its long red bill pries shellfish open and cuts the muscle before the shell shuts.
black-oystercatcher.role: A rocky-shore specialist that pries mussels and limpets from the rocks, timing feeding to the tides. It is a sensitive indicator of intertidal health, thriving only where shellfish are plentiful.

sources.name: All About Birds - Black Oystercatcher Life History

purple-shore-crab.diet: Sea lettuce and other green algae, plus occasional carrion
purple-shore-crab.fact: They scrape green algae from rocks and scuttle sideways under stones at low tide.
purple-shore-crab.role: A small grazing crab that scrapes algae from intertidal rocks and occasionally scavenges. It is common prey for gulls, anemones, and tidepool fish, moving algal energy up the food web.

brant-goose.diet: Eelgrass and large green algae like sea lettuce
brant-goose.preferredHabitat: Shallow coastal bays with eelgrass beds
brant-goose.fact: Whole flocks of brant depend on eelgrass beds to fuel their long migrations.
brant-goose.role: A small sea goose that grazes almost entirely on eelgrass and green algae in shallow bays. Its dependence on eelgrass makes healthy brant flocks a clear indicator of intact seagrass beds.

sources.name: All About Birds - Brant Life History

snowy-plover.diet: Beach invertebrates: crustaceans, flies, and small mollusks
snowy-plover.preferredHabitat: Quiet sandy dunes and open beach
snowy-plover.fact: Western snowy plovers nest in tiny scrapes right on the open sand.
snowy-plover.role: A threatened beach-nesting plover that feeds on small invertebrates along the sand and tide line. Extremely sensitive to disturbance, it is a flagship indicator of protected, undisturbed dune beaches.

sources.name: All About Birds - Snowy Plover Life History

annas-hummingbird.shelter: Shrubs and small trees in coastal scrub
annas-hummingbird.fact: Males dive from about 27 m and pull up with a loud chirp made by their tail feathers.
annas-hummingbird.role: A year-round coastal hummingbird that feeds on nectar and small insects, pollinating shrubs like manzanita and gooseberry as it forages. It links flowering coastal scrub to the wider food web.

sources.name: All About Birds - Anna's Hummingbird Life History

acorn-woodpecker.diet: Acorns and insects, plus sap and fruit
acorn-woodpecker.shelter: Oak granary trees with stored acorns
acorn-woodpecker.fact: It drills thousands of holes in a granary tree and stores a single acorn in each.
acorn-woodpecker.role: A social woodpecker that hoards acorns in shared granary trees and hawks flying insects. Its acorn caching and old cavities support other coastal-woodland animals, making it a habitat keystone in oak groves.

sources.name: All About Birds - Acorn Woodpecker Life History

black-turnstone.diet: Barnacles, limpets, mussels, and small invertebrates
black-turnstone.fact: Turnstones flip over stones and shells to snatch the creatures hiding beneath.
black-turnstone.role: A rocky-shore forager that pries barnacles and limpets loose and flips wrack to find hidden prey. It helps keep intertidal invertebrate numbers in check and depends on rich rocky shores.

sources.name: All About Birds - Black Turnstone Life History

pigeon-guillemot.diet: Small fish, plus crabs, worms, and mollusks
pigeon-guillemot.shelter: Bluff and rock crevices above water
pigeon-guillemot.preferredHabitat: Rocky nesting bluffs over clear water
pigeon-guillemot.fact: Pigeon guillemots have bright coral-red feet and matching mouth linings.
pigeon-guillemot.role: A diving seabird that chases small fish and pries invertebrates from crevices near the seafloor. It nests in rocky bluffs and depends on the healthy nearshore fish and habitat that kelp forests support.

sources.name: All About Birds - Pigeon Guillemot Life History

bat-star.diet: Algae, detritus, and dead plants and animals
bat-star.fact: A bat star can have anywhere from four to nine arms, not always five.
bat-star.role: An omnivorous scavenger that spreads its stomach over the seafloor to digest algae and carrion. It is a cleanup crew of the shallows, recycling dead matter and keeping tidepools and eelgrass beds tidy.

cottontail-rabbit.diet: Grasses and clover in summer; twigs, bark, and buds in winter
cottontail-rabbit.shelter: Rests in shallow grass 'forms'; uses brush piles and old burrows
cottontail-rabbit.preferredHabitat: Meadows and field edges with brushy fencerows to bolt into
cottontail-rabbit.fact: Cottontails rest in shallow ground depressions called 'forms' rather than digging their own burrows.
cottontail-rabbit.role: An abundant grazing herbivore and cornerstone prey animal of the meadow. It feeds on grasses, clover, and woody browse and breeds rapidly to offset heavy predation. Foxes, hawks, owls, and badgers all depend on cottontails as a food source.

monarch-butterfly.diet: Caterpillars eat only milkweed; adults sip flower nectar
monarch-butterfly.shelter: Roosts in trees and shrubs; overwinters clustered in dense groves
monarch-butterfly.preferredHabitat: Open meadows and roadsides with milkweed and nectar flowers
monarch-butterfly.fact: Monarchs migrate up to 3,000 miles, but no single butterfly makes the whole round trip; it takes several generations.
monarch-butterfly.role: A milkweed specialist and iconic pollinator whose caterpillars sequester the plant's cardenolide toxins, making both larvae and adults poisonous to most predators. Their bright orange warning coloration keeps nearly all birds and mammals away, so they have very few predators. Adults are important late-season nectar visitors.

sources.name: PNAS — Cardenolide sequestration and toxicity in monarchs

song-sparrow.diet: Insects and invertebrates in summer; seeds and fruits year-round
song-sparrow.shelter: Cup nest hidden on the ground or low in shrubs and grass tussocks
song-sparrow.preferredHabitat: Brushy edges, weedy fields, and marsh edges with singing perches
song-sparrow.fact: A male Song Sparrow can learn up to about 20 different tunes and sing hundreds of variations of them.
song-sparrow.role: A ground-foraging omnivore that switches between insects in the breeding season and seeds/fruit the rest of the year, so it both controls insects and disperses seeds. Its abundance makes it a key prey item for meadow hawks and snakes, linking ground invertebrates to larger predators.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Song Sparrow Life History

mule-deer.diet: Browses shrubs, forbs, twigs, buds, and seasonal grasses
mule-deer.shelter: Beds in brushy cover, tall grass, or forest edges; no permanent den
mule-deer.preferredHabitat: Open meadows and shrublands with browse and water nearby
mule-deer.fact: Mule deer are named for their oversized, mule-like ears, which rotate independently to pinpoint the direction of danger.
mule-deer.role: A large grazing herbivore that shapes meadow vegetation by browsing shrubs and forbs. Its grazing and droppings help cycle nutrients and keep browse in check. Its usual predators (coyotes, mountain lions) are absent from this meadow roster, so it faces little predation here.

sources.name: Landmark Wildlife — Mule Deer ears and senses

red-fox-meadow.diet: Voles, rabbits, squirrels, birds, and insects; also berries and carrion
red-fox-meadow.shelter: Digs earthen dens or enlarges burrows; uses brush and hollows
red-fox-meadow.preferredHabitat: Meadows, farmland edges, and hedgerows across open country
red-fox-meadow.fact: When 'mousing,' red foxes tend to pounce facing magnetic northeast, apparently using Earth's magnetic field as a rangefinder to judge the leap.
red-fox-meadow.role: A generalist mesopredator that helps control rodent and rabbit populations, hunting by stalk-and-pounce and rounding out its diet with insects, berries, and carrion. With larger predators like coyotes absent from this roster, it sits near the top of the meadow food web.

sources.name: Phys.org — Predation by foxes aided by Earth's magnetic field

meadow-vole.diet: Herbivore; grasses, sedges, seeds, roots, and bark in winter
meadow-vole.shelter: Shallow burrows and grass nests linked by surface runways
meadow-vole.preferredHabitat: Moist grassy meadows and fields with dense ground cover
meadow-vole.fact: Voles mow narrow 'runways' through the grass — tidy little highways they patrol between burrow openings.
meadow-vole.role: A keystone prey species and prolific breeder that converts meadow plants into food for nearly every predator. Its grazing and runway-building shape the grass layer. Its abundance drives the populations of hawks, owls, foxes, snakes, and badgers.

ground-squirrel.diet: Mostly seeds, grasses, and flowers, plus insects like grasshoppers
ground-squirrel.shelter: Extensive multi-entrance burrow systems dug in open ground
ground-squirrel.preferredHabitat: Open grassy meadows and slopes near rocky lookout points
ground-squirrel.fact: Facing a rattlesnake, these squirrels kick sand and wave heated tails — flushing their tails with blood to jam the snake's infrared 'vision.'
ground-squirrel.role: A burrowing omnivore whose diggings aerate soil and whose abandoned burrows shelter other species. It eats seeds, greens, and insects and is major prey for hawks, foxes, snakes, and badgers. Its colonies anchor the meadow's rodent-based food web.

sources.name: PNAS — Ground squirrels heat their tails to discourage rattlesnake attack
The Ethogram (UC Davis) — California ground squirrel

garter-snake-meadow.diet: Earthworms, amphibians, slugs, small fish, insects, and small rodents
garter-snake-meadow.shelter: Shelters under rocks and logs; overwinters in communal dens
garter-snake-meadow.preferredHabitat: Moist meadows and grasslands near sunny rocks and water
garter-snake-meadow.fact: Garter snakes are mildly venomous to their tiny prey but completely harmless to people.
garter-snake-meadow.role: A common meadow mesopredator that hunts earthworms, amphibians, fish, insects, and small rodents, using mild venomous saliva to subdue small prey. It helps control invertebrate and amphibian populations. It is preyed on by hawks, owls, and foxes.

sources.name: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service — Common Garter Snake

bumblebee.diet: Nectar for energy and pollen for protein, from many flower types
bumblebee.shelter: Nests in abandoned rodent burrows, grass tussocks, or ground cavities
bumblebee.preferredHabitat: Flower-rich meadows and grasslands with continuous bloom
bumblebee.fact: Bumblebees 'buzz pollinate' — vibrating their flight muscles to shake pollen loose from flowers like tomatoes and blueberries.
bumblebee.role: A generalist, large-bodied pollinator that visits a huge variety of flowers for nectar and pollen. Its buzz pollination unlocks pollen that many other bees cannot reach, making it vital to meadow plant reproduction. It is preyed on by ambush hunters and aerial insectivores.

grasshopper.diet: Herbivore feeding on grasses, sedges, and broadleaf forbs
grasshopper.shelter: Shelters in grass and low vegetation; lays eggs in soil
grasshopper.preferredHabitat: Sunny grasslands and meadows rich in grasses and forbs
grasshopper.fact: Grasshoppers hear through tympana — eardrum-like membranes on the first segment of the abdomen, not their heads.
grasshopper.role: A dominant plant-eater and the meadow's key prey base, converting grasses and forbs into food for a huge range of predators. Its abundance supports birds, snakes, mammals, and other insects. Booms in grasshopper numbers ripple up the whole food web.

sources.name: Ecology and Evolution — Grasshopper diet (gut-content sequencing)

lady-beetle.diet: Predator of aphids and other small, soft-bodied insects
lady-beetle.shelter: Overwinters in leaf litter and aggregations; shelters on foliage
lady-beetle.preferredHabitat: Meadows and gardens with aphid-infested plants
lady-beetle.fact: A single lady beetle can eat around 5,000 aphids over its lifetime — roughly 50 a day.
lady-beetle.role: A voracious small predator that controls aphids and other soft-bodied pests as both larva and adult, making it a valuable biological-control insect. In turn it is eaten by insectivorous birds and larger insect predators, linking the aphid layer up into the food web.

sources.name: UC ANR — Lady beetle aphid consumption

western-meadowlark.diet: Mostly insects in summer (beetles, grasshoppers); seeds and grain in winter
western-meadowlark.shelter: Domed grass nest woven on the ground, often with a covered runway
western-meadowlark.preferredHabitat: Wide native grasslands and meadows with song perches
western-meadowlark.fact: The Western Meadowlark's flute-like song is the state bird anthem of six U.S. states.
western-meadowlark.role: A grassland omnivore that eats large numbers of grasshoppers, crickets, and beetles in summer while taking seeds in winter, helping keep insect populations in check. As a plump ground bird it is important prey for hawks and mammalian predators of the meadow.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Western Meadowlark

barn-swallow.diet: Flying insects caught midair: flies, beetles, bees, wasps, and moths
barn-swallow.shelter: Cup nest of mud pellets and grass on beams under eaves and bridges
barn-swallow.preferredHabitat: Open country for foraging near water, flowers, and structures
barn-swallow.fact: Barn Swallows build their cup nests from up to 1,000 individual beakfuls of mud.
barn-swallow.role: An aerial insectivore that snaps up huge numbers of flying insects over meadows, following livestock and machinery to catch flushed prey. It is a natural check on flies and flying pests, and both adults and fledglings are hunted by fast-flying hawks.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Barn Swallow Life History

red-tailed-hawk.diet: Mostly small mammals (voles, ground squirrels, rabbits); also birds and snakes
red-tailed-hawk.shelter: Bulky stick nest in the crown of a tall tree or on a cliff ledge
red-tailed-hawk.preferredHabitat: Open country: grasslands, fields, and meadows seen from above
red-tailed-hawk.fact: That piercing 'eagle' cry in the movies is almost always actually a Red-tailed Hawk.
red-tailed-hawk.role: The meadow's apex daytime hunter, soaring on broad wings or watching from a perch for prey below. By preying on voles, ground squirrels, rabbits, and birds it keeps herbivore numbers in check. Adults have essentially no predators in the meadow.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Red-tailed Hawk Life History
Cornell Lab All About Birds — Red-tailed Hawk Overview

barn-owl.diet: Almost entirely small mammals — voles, mice, and shrews; hunted at night
barn-owl.shelter: Nests in tree hollows, cliff crevices, and quiet building cavities
barn-owl.preferredHabitat: Open grasslands and meadows hunted on silent wings at night
barn-owl.fact: A Barn Owl's heart-shaped facial disc funnels sound so precisely it can catch prey in total darkness by ear alone.
barn-owl.role: The meadow's night-shift rodent hunter, coursing low over the grass on silent wings and swallowing voles and mice whole. This makes it a major check on rodent populations. In the meadow it sits near the top of the food web with no regular predators.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Barn Owl Life History

american-goldfinch.diet: Almost entirely seeds — thistle, sunflower, aster, and grass seeds
american-goldfinch.shelter: Tightly woven cup nest lashed high in a shrub with spider silk
american-goldfinch.preferredHabitat: Weedy fields and open areas with thistle, sunflower, and asters
american-goldfinch.fact: Goldfinches are strict vegetarians and nest late in summer so thistle down is ready to line their nests.
american-goldfinch.role: A specialist granivore that thrives on thistle and other composite seeds, making it an important disperser of weedy plant seeds across the meadow. Being small and abundant, it is prey for agile bird-hunting hawks and small owls.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — American Goldfinch Life History

eastern-bluebird.diet: Mainly ground insects (caterpillars, beetles, grasshoppers); fruit in winter
eastern-bluebird.shelter: Grass-lined nest inside tree cavities, old woodpecker holes, or boxes
eastern-bluebird.preferredHabitat: Grassy openings with scattered trees and perches to hunt from
eastern-bluebird.fact: Eastern Bluebirds can spot a tiny insect in the grass from about 60 feet away, then drop down to grab it.
eastern-bluebird.role: A cavity-nesting insectivore that hunts caterpillars, beetles, and grasshoppers from perches, switching to berries in winter, both controlling insects and dispersing fruit seeds. It competes for nest holes and is preyed on by hawks and small owls.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Eastern Bluebird Life History

leafcutter-bee.diet: Adults eat nectar and pollen from many flowering plants
leafcutter-bee.shelter: Nests in hollow stems and soil, lining cells with cut leaf pieces
leafcutter-bee.preferredHabitat: Meadows and gardens with diverse flowers and nesting cavities
leafcutter-bee.fact: Female leafcutter bees snip neat circles from leaves to build and seal their nest cells.
leafcutter-bee.role: A solitary native bee that pollinates a wide range of meadow and crop plants, carrying pollen on the underside of its abdomen. Its leaf-lined nest cells provision the next generation with pollen and nectar. Adults are caught by ambush predators and aerial insectivores.

sources.name: USDA Forest Service — Leafcutter Bees (Megachile spp.)

painted-lady.diet: Adults nectar on composite flowers; caterpillars eat thistles and mallows
painted-lady.shelter: Rests on vegetation; caterpillars build silk nests on host plants
painted-lady.preferredHabitat: Open meadows and disturbed ground with thistles and nectar flowers
painted-lady.fact: Painted ladies migrate thousands of miles across continents — one of the most widespread butterflies on Earth.
painted-lady.role: A wide-ranging migratory butterfly and generalist nectar pollinator whose caterpillars feed on thistles, mallows, and over 100 other host plants. Population booms can trigger massive migrations. Adults and larvae are eaten by birds, wasps, and spiders.

sources.name: Butterflies and Moths of North America — Painted Lady

american-badger.diet: Digs out ground squirrels, gophers, voles, and mice; also insects
american-badger.shelter: Digs its own large underground burrows; a powerful excavator
american-badger.preferredHabitat: Open meadows and grasslands with diggable soil and rodent prey
american-badger.fact: Badgers sometimes team up with coyotes: the badger digs prey out below while the coyote catches those that bolt above ground.
american-badger.role: A fossorial carnivore that hunts by digging burrowing rodents straight out of their tunnels, keeping ground squirrel and vole numbers down. Its abandoned burrows benefit other animals. Adult badgers have essentially no predators in this meadow.

coopers-hawk.diet: Mainly medium and small birds; also chipmunks, mice, and squirrels
coopers-hawk.shelter: Builds a stick nest high in a tree, on a limb or in a crotch
coopers-hawk.preferredHabitat: Woodland edges and open country with scattered trees near meadows
coopers-hawk.fact: Cooper's Hawks thread through dense cover at high speed to ambush songbirds — a risky style that leaves many with healed chest-bone fractures.
coopers-hawk.role: A bird-hunting mesopredator that patrols meadow edges and thickets for songbirds. Its agile, low pursuit flight lets it pluck sparrows, finches, and bluebirds from cover. It controls small-bird numbers but can itself be displaced by larger raptors.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Cooper's Hawk Life History
Cornell Lab All About Birds — Cooper's Hawk Overview

western-screech-owl.diet: Small mammals and large insects; also small birds and worms
western-screech-owl.shelter: Roosts and nests in tree cavities, old woodpecker holes, and boxes
western-screech-owl.preferredHabitat: Wooded edges and brushy areas bordering open meadows
western-screech-owl.fact: This pint-sized owl occasionally takes prey larger than itself, including cottontail rabbits.
western-screech-owl.role: A small nocturnal mesopredator that sits and waits, then drops onto rodents and insects, gleaning grasshoppers and beetles and snatching voles and mice on the ground. It bridges insect and rodent control in the meadow at night.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Western Screech-Owl Life History
Cornell Lab All About Birds — Western Screech-Owl Overview

praying-mantis.diet: Ambush predator eating live insects — bees, grasshoppers, and more
praying-mantis.shelter: Perches motionless on plants; lays eggs in a foam egg case (ootheca)
praying-mantis.preferredHabitat: Meadows and shrubby edges with dense vegetation for ambush
praying-mantis.fact: A praying mantis can swivel its head almost 180 degrees — unique among insects — for a wide field of view.
praying-mantis.role: A sit-and-wait ambush mesopredator that seizes prey with spined forelegs in a strike faster than a blink. As a generalist it eats grasshoppers, bees, beetles, and other insects, helping regulate insect numbers. It is itself taken by birds, garter snakes, and small owls.

killdeer.diet: Invertebrates — earthworms, grasshoppers, beetles, and snails
killdeer.shelter: Nests in a bare ground scrape lined with pebbles and shell bits
killdeer.preferredHabitat: Open, flat ground with very short grass and scattered stones
killdeer.fact: Killdeer fake a broken wing, dragging it as if injured to lure predators away from the nest.
killdeer.role: A ground-foraging insectivore that races and halts across open meadow, snapping up worms and insects. As abundant, exposed ground-nesters they are important prey for meadow hunters, which take adults, chicks, and eggs alike.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Killdeer Life History

red-admiral.diet: Adults prefer tree sap, fermenting fruit, and nectar; caterpillars eat nettles
red-admiral.shelter: Caterpillars fold nettle leaves into shelters; adults roost on trees
red-admiral.preferredHabitat: Flowery clearings and woodland edges near nettle patches
red-admiral.fact: Red admirals are bold and territorial, and will readily land and perch on people who stay still.
red-admiral.role: A fast, territorial butterfly that feeds mainly on tree sap, fruit, and dung, visiting flowers as a nectar pollinator when preferred foods are scarce; its caterpillars specialize on stinging nettles. Lacking chemical defenses, it relies on camouflage and speed to escape birds and other predators.

sources.name: USDA Forest Service — Red Admiral Butterfly
Butterflies and Moths of North America — Red Admiral

desert-cottontail.diet: Grasses, mesquite, cactus pads, and other desert plants
desert-cottontail.shelter: Brush cover and borrowed or natural burrows
desert-cottontail.preferredHabitat: Brushy flats with shade and open forage
desert-cottontail.fact: Desert cottontails get most of their water from the plants they eat.
desert-cottontail.role: A common desert herbivore that grazes grasses and browse. It is a cornerstone prey species, feeding foxes, coyotes, bobcats, and raptors. Its abundance helps support the desert's predators.

kit-fox.diet: Kangaroo rats, rabbits, insects, and occasional fruit
kit-fox.shelter: Cool underground dens with several entrances
kit-fox.preferredHabitat: Open desert with abundant small prey
kit-fox.fact: The smallest wild dog in North America, its huge ears both hear prey and shed heat.
kit-fox.role: A small nocturnal desert canid and mesopredator that hunts rodents and rabbits. It seldom needs to drink, getting moisture from prey. Coyotes are its main threat.

coyote.diet: Rodents, rabbits, fruit, carrion, and insects
coyote.preferredHabitat: Open desert with prey and cover
coyote.fact: The most vocal wild mammal in North America; a howling pack sounds like many more.
coyote.role: The desert's most adaptable predator, an omnivore taking rodents, rabbits, fruit, and carrion. It is the top mammalian predator here and the main killer of kit foxes. Its howls carry for miles at dusk.

kangaroo-rat.shelter: Deep burrow systems in loose soil
kangaroo-rat.fact: Kangaroo rats never sweat or pant and get by on water made from the dry seeds they eat.
kangaroo-rat.role: A seed-eating rodent and key desert prey species. It caches seeds underground, shaping which plants grow. It feeds nearly every desert predator, from rattlesnakes to owls to foxes.

jackrabbit.diet: Grasses, cactus, and woody twigs and bark
jackrabbit.fact: A jackrabbit's enormous ears act like radiators, releasing body heat to keep it cool.
jackrabbit.role: A fast, open-country herbivore that browses grasses, twigs, and cactus. It is major prey for coyotes, bobcats, and large raptors. Its big ears both hear predators and dump heat.

roadrunner.diet: Lizards, insects, scorpions, and small snakes
roadrunner.shelter: Low nests in brush and cactus
roadrunner.preferredHabitat: Open hunting ground with brushy edges
roadrunner.fact: It slams large prey against rocks to break the bones, and will kill and eat rattlesnakes.
roadrunner.role: A ground-running predatory bird that sprints down lizards, insects, scorpions, and snakes. It is a key mesopredator on small desert reptiles and arthropods. Coyotes and hawks hunt it.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Greater Roadrunner

burrowing-owl.shelter: Underground burrows dug by other animals
burrowing-owl.preferredHabitat: Burrow mounds with open hunting space
burrowing-owl.fact: It hisses a raspy call that mimics a rattlesnake to scare intruders out of its burrow.
burrowing-owl.role: A small ground-dwelling owl that nests in borrowed burrows and hunts insects by day and rodents at night. It is both an insectivore and a mesopredator on small mammals. Badgers and coyotes prey on it.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Burrowing Owl

gambels-quail.fact: A male sentinel calls from a perch while the rest of the covey feeds below.
gambels-quail.role: A social, ground-feeding quail that eats seeds, greens, and cactus fruit. It is important prey for coyotes, bobcats, and desert hawks. Coveys post a lookout while the flock forages.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Gambel's Quail

desert-tortoise.preferredHabitat: Native plants with shade and burrow ground
desert-tortoise.fact: Desert tortoises can live 80 years and spend up to 98% of their lives in burrows.
desert-tortoise.role: A long-lived herbivore and ecosystem engineer. Its burrows, which can exceed 10 metres, shelter snakes, lizards, rodents, and insects. Adults are nearly predator-free, but eggs and young are widely eaten.

horned-lizard.diet: Mostly ants, plus other small insects
horned-lizard.preferredHabitat: Sunny open ground near ant trails
horned-lizard.fact: Texas horned lizards can squirt a jet of blood from their eyes to startle predators.
horned-lizard.role: A specialist insectivore that feeds mainly on harvester ants, with a large stomach to process them. It is prey for roadrunners, hawks, shrikes, and snakes. Its blood-squirting defense targets canid predators.

collared-lizard.fact: Collared lizards sprint on their hind legs like tiny dinosaurs, tail streaming behind.
collared-lizard.role: An active, sit-and-wait predator of insects and smaller lizards among the rocks. It is a mesopredator on desert arthropods and hatchling reptiles. Hawks, snakes, and roadrunners prey on it.

rattlesnake.preferredHabitat: Rocky shelter near busy rodent trails
rattlesnake.fact: It adds a rattle segment at each shed, but segments break, so you can't count its age.
rattlesnake.role: A venomous ambush predator and key control on desert rodent populations. It swallows prey whole and eats only every few weeks. Roadrunners, hawks, and coyotes are among its predators.

tarantula.fact: A desert tarantula may live 25 years, most of it within a few feet of one burrow.
tarantula.role: A long-lived, nocturnal ambush predator of insects and other invertebrates from its burrow. It is a mesopredator on desert arthropods. Birds, snakes, and the tarantula hawk wasp prey on it.

scorpion.diet: Insects, spiders, and other small invertebrates
scorpion.shelter: Burrows and cover under rocks and bark
scorpion.preferredHabitat: Rocky cover with night hunting ground
scorpion.fact: Scorpions glow blue-green under ultraviolet light, and no one is entirely sure why.
scorpion.role: The largest scorpion in North America, a nocturnal ambush predator of insects, spiders, and even other scorpions. It is a mesopredator on desert arthropods and small prey. Owls, lizards, and roadrunners hunt it.

desert-bee.fact: Solitary cactus bees nest alone but gather by the thousands in shared ground colonies.
desert-bee.role: A solitary native bee and key pollinator of desert cacti such as prickly pear and cholla. As a herbivore on nectar and pollen, it sustains cactus reproduction. Lizards, birds, and spiders prey on it.

gila-woodpecker.fact: Its abandoned saguaro cavities later shelter elf owls, pygmy-owls, and kestrels.
gila-woodpecker.role: A cactus-nesting woodpecker and desert keystone builder. It eats insects, cactus fruit, and berries, and its old nest holes house many other desert animals. Hawks, snakes, and bobcats prey on it.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Gila Woodpecker

cactus-wren.fact: Cactus wrens use their football-shaped cholla nests year-round, even sleeping in them.
cactus-wren.role: The largest North American wren, an insectivore gleaning spiders and insects and taking cactus fruit. It gets most of its water from food. Snakes, roadrunners, and hawks prey on it and its nests.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Cactus Wren

desert-iguana.diet: Flowers, buds, and leaves, especially creosote
desert-iguana.fact: Desert iguanas stay active near 40C, heat that drives other lizards into the shade.
desert-iguana.role: A heat-loving herbivorous lizard that feeds mainly on creosote bush flowers and leaves. It is a desert plant grazer and prey for snakes, raptors, and foxes. It shelters in burrows through the hottest hours.

kangaroo-mouse.fact: It survives on water made from its food and may go a lifetime without ever drinking.
kangaroo-mouse.role: A tiny seed-eating rodent that stores fat in its tail for lean times. It is prey for rattlesnakes, owls, and foxes, making it part of the base of the desert food web. It rarely if ever needs to drink.

banded-gecko.fact: Unlike most geckos, the banded gecko has movable eyelids and squeaks when captured.
banded-gecko.role: A small nocturnal gecko that hunts insects, spiders, and even young scorpions. It is a mesopredator on tiny desert prey and food for larger lizards, snakes, and roadrunners. It sheds its tail to escape.

sources.name: Arizona-Sonora Desert Museum — Western Banded Gecko

costas-hummingbird.fact: Courting males dive past a female with a shrill whistle, flashing violet throat feathers.
costas-hummingbird.role: A small desert hummingbird that feeds on nectar from agave, chuparosa, and other blooms plus tiny insects. It is an important pollinator and a nectar-feeding herbivore. Snakes and predatory birds take it.

elf-owl.fact: The world's smallest owl plucks the stinger off scorpions before eating them.
elf-owl.role: The world's smallest owl, a nocturnal insectivore that hunts insects and scorpions and nests in old woodpecker holes. It is a mesopredator on desert arthropods. Snakes and larger owls threaten it.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Elf Owl
Cornell Lab All About Birds — Elf Owl Overview

chuckwalla.fact: A threatened chuckwalla wedges into a crack and inflates its lungs to lock itself in.
chuckwalla.role: A large herbivorous lizard that grazes desert leaves, flowers, and fruit among boulders. It is a plant-eater and prey for hawks, kestrels, coyotes, and rattlesnakes. Its lung-inflation defense locks it into crevices.

phainopepla.fact: The phainopepla is desert mistletoe's key seed disperser; the two depend on each other.
phainopepla.role: A glossy desert songbird whose winter diet is mostly desert mistletoe berries, plus insects caught on the wing. It is a crucial mistletoe seed disperser and a fruit-and-insect omnivore. Snakes and raptors prey on it.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Phainopepla

antelope-squirrel.fact: It carries its tail arched over its back like a parasol to shade itself from the sun.
antelope-squirrel.role: A diurnal, heat-tolerant omnivore that eats seeds, greens, fruit, and insects even in midday heat. It is prey for hawks, foxes, bobcats, and snakes. It shades itself with its tail and dumps heat on cool ground.

beaver.diet: Bark and cambium of willow and aspen, plus aquatic plants
beaver.preferredHabitat: Slow channels with mud banks and woody plants to fell
beaver.fact: Beaver dams create wetlands that store water and support hundreds of other species.
beaver.role: The wetland's ecosystem engineer. By felling trees and building dams, beavers flood new ponds, raise the water table, and create habitat that most other marsh species depend on.

river-otter.diet: Fish, crayfish, frogs, and other aquatic animals
river-otter.preferredHabitat: Clean water rich with fish and slow prey
river-otter.fact: River otters can hold their breath underwater for up to eight minutes while hunting.
river-otter.role: An agile aquatic mesopredator that patrols channels for fish and crayfish. Otters keep fish and amphibian numbers in check and are a sign of clean, well-connected water.

muskrat.diet: Mainly cattails, reeds, and roots; sometimes clams and small fish
muskrat.shelter: Dome lodges woven from reeds, and bank burrows
muskrat.fact: Muskrats can stay underwater for up to 15 minutes on a single breath.
muskrat.role: A mostly plant-eating rodent that clips reeds and cattails, opening water lanes used by ducks and other marsh life. It is important prey for mink and otters.

mink.diet: Fish, frogs, crayfish, and small mammals like muskrats
mink.shelter: Bank burrows, often taken over from muskrats
mink.fact: Mink can swim up to 30 metres underwater when chasing prey.
mink.role: A fierce semi-aquatic hunter that takes fish, frogs, and even muskrats. Mink are versatile mesopredators that help regulate small wetland prey.

great-blue-heron.diet: Fish, frogs, and small aquatic animals; also voles and other birds
great-blue-heron.shelter: Colonial stick nests high in trees near water
great-blue-heron.preferredHabitat: Still shallows for slow, patient hunting
great-blue-heron.fact: A great blue heron can strike like lightning to spear a fish or snap up a vole.
great-blue-heron.role: The tall, patient sentinel of the shallows and a top predator of the wetland's fish community. It stalks slowly, then strikes faster than the eye can follow.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds - Great Blue Heron

mallard-duck.diet: Seeds and aquatic plants, plus insect larvae, snails, and worms
mallard-duck.shelter: Ground nests hidden in reedy water edges
mallard-duck.fact: Mallards can sleep with one eye open, resting half their brain at a time.
mallard-duck.role: A dabbling omnivore that tips forward to feed on seeds, plants, and small invertebrates. Its ducklings and eggs feed many marsh predators.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds - Mallard

red-winged-blackbird.diet: Insects in summer, seeds and grain the rest of the year
red-winged-blackbird.shelter: Cup nests woven into standing reeds
red-winged-blackbird.preferredHabitat: Dense reed beds and cattail marsh
red-winged-blackbird.fact: Male red-winged blackbirds can hide or flash their scarlet shoulder patches at will.
red-winged-blackbird.role: An abundant, noisy marsh songbird that eats insects and seeds. Males fiercely defend reed-bed territories that may hold a dozen nests.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds - Red-winged Blackbird

sandhill-crane.diet: Grains, tubers, insects, and small animals
sandhill-crane.shelter: Large ground mounds of marsh plants near standing water
sandhill-crane.fact: Sandhill cranes mate for life and choose partners through leaping, bowing dances.
sandhill-crane.role: A stately omnivore of open marsh that probes for tubers and grain and snaps up insects and small animals. Its presence signals a wide, healthy wetland.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds - Sandhill Crane

painted-turtle.diet: Aquatic plants, insects, small fish, and carrion
painted-turtle.shelter: Muddy pond bottoms; basks on logs
painted-turtle.fact: Painted turtles overwinter under the ice, taking in oxygen through their skin.
